rv.q: Now the play resounds with a chilling immediacy that lends it even greater and more unsettling power.
Prayer for the French Republic asks big questions – of history, of family, of identity – and, all but miraculously, answers their call.
Whatever your identity, rarely in a Broadway theater will you have so powerfully felt your own vulnerability.
Harmon meticulously architects characters so personable and living-room spats so heightened that you'll question for a moment if you're not fighting with relatives in your own home.
Yet there’s a savviness to Prayer’s construction that makes it ring false.
By the third act, the arguments have stripped their gears completely, and the play ends in sentimental exhaustion.
Harmon too often fails to make his characters into anything other than animated position papers.
By comparison, flaws that were already noticeable Off Broadway seem more pronounced.

But it doesn’t tell it in a compelling or nuanced manner — despite Harmon having set himself up to succeed with a flashback story that could, but does not, provide real context and present-day interlocutors who could, but do not, push the Benhamous beyond platitudes.
What you’ll get instead is a superb drama that only seems to have gained in power and intensity with this Broadway transfer.
He digs deeper than ever in Prayer for the French Republic and strikes pure gold.
You will not soon forget these characters or the difficult decision they face as they struggle with what is yet another piece of the endlessly complex immigrants' story.
The acting is stellar and the comedy is perfectly placed.
Prayer for the French Republic is a powerful reminder that a better future is only possible if you live to have a future.
It’s the almost-ideal match of the personal and the political, especially as brought to vivid life by a superb ensemble cast under David Cromer’s razor-sharp direction.
What keeps the play riveting is the vigor with which Harmon considers every side of the central question, creating confrontations from which nobody emerges unscathed.
Criticisms aside, The French Republic is a must see for anyone who’s interested in deepening their understanding of the Jewish experience through the ages.
As well-constructed as many of the scenes are, there is too much going on; too much the playwright is trying to do.
A tighter structure and a shorter run time would help greatly but, even as it is, audiences will find much here to appreciate and from which to learn.
Prayer bitterly reminds us that all of this has happened before, and most likely will again.
The intergenerational trauma of the Holocaust was incredibly well expressed.

The play is engrossing and the cast breathes relatable life into morally knotty arguments that careen rapidly between the Holocaust, the Crusades, Israel-Palestine conflicts, terrorism, French colonialism, the rise of far-right leaders like LePen, and more.
Prayer for the French Republic combines the virtues of family drama, history lesson and the spark of the best Sunday-morning political panel shows.
Harmon is just trying to give us the answers.

cn.t: Harmon's ambitious three-hour drama about a French Jewish family grappling with antisemitism across generations earns strong praise for its timeliness and emotional power, though some critics find it overstuffed and structurally uneven.
